title: Cities terminate Flock contracts at record pace in August
gist: Advocacy group Secure Justice says cancellations of Flock Safety's surveillance-camera contracts by US cities and counties have gone parabolic, with 93 jurisdictions dropping Flock in August 2026 alone, even as the company claims new signings still outpace churn 10-to-1 and faces bipartisan political scrutiny including a Senate probe.

insights.claim: Secure Justice, an Oakland-based anti-surveillance advocacy group, has recorded 214 US cities and counties that have dropped Flock Safety camera contracts since 2021.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Establishes a multi-year baseline for Flock customer churn that investors or competitors can use to gauge contract stability in the ALPR surveillance-camera market.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Secure Justice, an Oakland-based advocacy group'

insights.claim: Of the 214 total jurisdictions that have dropped Flock since 2021, 93 ended their contracts in August 2026 alone, a fourfold increase over the previous month, averaging about three localities per day halting contracts over the prior 30 days.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A fourfold month-over-month acceleration in cancellations is a sharp leading indicator of reputational or regulatory risk materializing quickly for Flock's public-sector revenue base.
insights.quote: Looking at that image, it’s gone parabolic!

insights.claim: Brian Hofer, Secure Justice's executive director and former chair of the Oakland Privacy Advisory Commission, says that if the cancellation pace continues for another year it will represent 'serious money' lost for Flock.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A domain expert explicitly frames the churn trend as a near-term financial risk to Flock, not just a reputational or political story.
insights.quote: When you see that now 165 [cancellations] are just in the first almost eight months of this year… At that speed, if it goes another year, we’re talking serious money,

insights.claim: Flock Safety disputes that churn is a meaningful problem, saying new city partnerships have outpaced nonrenewals by roughly 10 to 1 so far in 2026, while declining to disclose the exact number of new customers signed.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Flock's refusal to disclose absolute new-customer numbers alongside a favorable ratio claim is a data-transparency gap investors should flag when assessing the churn narrative.
insights.quote: So far in 2026, new city partnerships have outpaced nonrenewals by approximately 10 to one,

insights.claim: Facing criticism, Flock CEO Garrett Langley announced the company would cut its default data retention period from 30 days to seven days.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A retroactive product concession on data retention signals Flock views the current backlash as material enough to change core product defaults, not just messaging.

insights.claim: Flock's top lawyer updated the company's terms of use to expressly prohibit customers and their users from using Flock services to mislead, harass, stalk, or otherwise violate another person's legal rights, but this has done little to quell political scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Contractual language changes are being tried as a liability shield but are not resolving the underlying trust deficit driving contract cancellations.
insights.quote: expressly prohibit customers and their users from using Flock Services to mislead, harass, stalk, or otherwise impose upon or violate the legal rights of another person.
insights.locator: paragraph on Flock's top lawyer blog post

insights.claim: Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) announced he is investigating Flock Safety's collection, retention, and dissemination of data generated by its AI surveillance cameras.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A Republican senator opening a federal inquiry indicates the backlash against Flock has become bipartisan, raising the odds of federal-level regulatory action beyond local contract losses.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This week, Sen. Josh Hawley'

insights.claim: After two Florida police officers were arrested for misusing Flock cameras, Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis said Flock cameras were 'out of control' in his state, citing an example of an officer using the system to track an ex-girlfriend.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Concrete police-misuse incidents are what's converting abstract privacy concerns into hard political opposition from officials across the political spectrum.
insights.quote: When I see, like, a police officer using this to track, like, an ex-girlfriend, I'm like, you know what the hell's going on?

insights.claim: Jake Laperruque of the Center for Democracy and Technology says AI is turning automated license plate readers into a mass surveillance dragnet, citing Flock's keyword/person search, cities adding real-time facial recognition to camera networks, and Border Patrol using AI on ALPR data to flag 'suspicious' driving patterns for stops.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Frames Flock's core risk as a capability escalation problem: AI features layered onto existing ALPR infrastructure expand surveillance scope well beyond what the cameras were originally sold to do.
insights.quote: And we're already seeing how AI can morph ALPRs into a mass surveillance dragnet. Flock lets its cameras be searched for keywords and people, cities are incorporating real-time facial recognition into camera networks, Border Patrol is using AI to scan ALPR data for driving patterns [and] pulling people over whenever the AI deems their driving 'suspicious.'

insights.claim: UC Berkeley law professor Catherine Crump cites documented abuses including a Texas Sheriff's Office using Flock-style technology to search for a woman who had had an abortion and federal agents proposing its use outside gun shows.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Specific documented misuse cases involving reproductive rights and gun-show surveillance are the kind of headline risk that keeps driving local contract cancellations regardless of Flock's stated new-signing pace.
insights.quote: A Texas Sheriff's Office used it to search for a woman who had had an abortion, and federal agents proposed using it outside gun shows.
